claim: With the 60x objective at 1.5x intermediate magnification and 1x1 binning, one pixel spans 0.07222 micrometres at the sample plane, measured by the operator on this instrument.

numbers.name: pixel_size
numbers.note: the table was headed um/px. A pixel size is a length -- the per-pixel is carried by the quantity's name, not the unit, and units.json has no per-pixel unit to carry it

valid_until.event:
the camera is replaced. Ruled by the person on 2026-09-21 (src_person_ruling_20260921); the date beside it is unchanged and is still the operator's stated fifteen years anchored to the report rather than to the measurement, because asked whether to re-anchor they had no preference.

THE MECHANISM, because a trigger on its own is not checkable: a pixel size at the sample plane is the sensor pitch divided by the total magnification, and the pitch belongs to the camera -- camera_sensor_geometry carries the Kinetix 22's 6.5 um. A different sensor moves the numerator of every row at once, which is why this is ONE event and not twelve: all twelve come from the single calibration cal-pixel-size-20260919 and end together.

AN OBJECTIVE CHANGE DOES NOT END THIS, and that near miss is worth naming here because it is the one a reader is most likely to assume. Each row carries its objective and intermediate magnification as `identifiers`, exact by definition, rather than as conditions -- so turning the nosepiece selects a different row instead of falsifying one (objective_change_selects_a_pixel_size_row). The store also holds objective_change_invalidates_trap_calibration, which says the opposite about a DIFFERENT calibration: the tweezers hold one pixel-to-micrometre calibration that a swap destroys.

IT TRIGGERS CONSERVATIVELY AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. cameras_both_kinetix22 records that both bodies on this bench are the same model and therefore share a pixel size, so swapping one Kinetix 22 for the other would fire this event without moving any value here. Over-triggering costs a re-check; under-triggering costs a number that is silently wrong, and nothing on this instrument would report it. The wording keeps the person's trigger rather than narrowing it to `a camera of a different pitch`, because narrowing it would make the expiry depend on a judgement about the replacement instead of on an observable event.

validity_conditions: This instrument, the 60x objective at 1.5x intermediate magnification, at 1x1 binning. The binning is in `validity` and not only here, because it is the one condition of this calibration that is a quantity: at 2x2 the value doubles, so a caller at another binning gets `partial` with the miss named rather than a number that is wrong by a factor. The objective and the zoom are nominal designations, exact by definition, so they are identifiers and not conditions. Valid for fifteen years as the operator stated, anchored to 2026-09-19 because the day the measurement was taken was not recorded -- the anchor is the report, not the event. What actually falsifies a pixel size is not elapsed time but a change to the optical chain: swapping this objective, changing the camera, altering the intermediate magnification. This instrument's paper record has diverged from its hardware before, so the period is the operator's statement and the falsifier is the thing to watch. What the set relates by, recorded because it is checkable and the next reader will find it. Every 1.5x value is the 1x value of the same objective divided by exactly 1.5, to the digits given, and five of the six 1x values equal 6.5 um over the nominal magnification. The exception is the 20x, whose 0.32373 implies 6.5/0.32373 = 20.078 -- the figure plan.md 1950 names as the prior project's artifact, a calibrated quantity stored wearing a nominal name. The operator was shown this and confirmed all twelve are direct measurements. Both facts are recorded: what the numbers relate by, and that they were measured independently. Nothing here back-derives a magnification -- 20x is the nominal designation, a string identifier, and 20.078 is not stored as one.
